_note: Maths reasoning cases: a situation, the information given, a question and candidate answers, in two versions. Solve, where the numbers settle it and every wrong answer is ruled out by a line of the problem. Debate, where a line has been changed and more than one answer holds up if the student says what it assumes. Written by hand in scripts/math-cases/g<N>.json and folded together by scripts/merge-math-cases.mjs; do not edit this file by hand. scripts/check-math-cases.mjs re-derives every solve answer and holds the structure to its rules.

cases.title: The Case of the Empty Chair
given: 8 children came to story time.
There are 6 chairs in the circle.
Every child wants a chair.
Nobody brings in more chairs.
cases.question: How many children have no chair?

rules_out.why: 6 is how many chairs there are, not how many children are left standing.
8 is every child who came, and 6 of them do get a chair.
Only 8 children came, so 14 of them cannot be left out.

cases.explain: Match one child to one chair. Six pairs up, and the children left over are the answer: 8 take away 6 is 2.

given: 8 children came to story time.
There are 6 chairs in the circle.
2 children chose to sit on the rug.
1 chair is broken and wobbles.
debate.question: How many children have no chair? Say which words you used.

arguments.why: 8 children and 6 chairs leaves 2 children standing.
A broken chair is not a chair to sit on, so only 5 of them work: 8 take away 5 is 3.
2 children chose the rug, so the other 6 each had one of the 6 chairs and nobody was left out.

debate.note: All three can be argued. What settles it is what counts as a chair and what counts as wanting one, so make the child say which words they used.

cases.title: The Case of the Last Number Said
given: Ana counts the blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
She touches one block for each number she says.
She does not miss a block.
She does not touch any block twice.
cases.question: How many blocks are there?

rules_out.why: 1 is the first number Ana said, and she kept going after it.
4 is the number before the last one. She touched a block after she said it.
15 adds up all the numbers she said. Counting says each number once, it does not collect them.

cases.explain: The last number you say when you count is how many there are. Ana said 5 last, and she touched one block for each number, so there are 5 blocks.

given: Ana counts the blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
She touched one block two times.
There is a block under the table.
Ana says there are 5.
debate.question: How many blocks are there? Say how you know.

arguments.why: She said 5, but she touched one block two times, so only 4 blocks were on the table.
4 on the table and 1 under it makes 5, so Ana's answer is right even though her counting was not.

debate.note: Ana gets 5 and 5 may well be correct, for a reason that has nothing to do with how she counted. Worth saying out loud: a right answer and good counting are two different things.

cases.title: The Case of the Full Frame
given: There are 13 counters on the mat.
10 counters fill the ten-frame.
The rest sit outside the frame.
Every counter is on the mat somewhere.
cases.question: How many counters are outside the frame?

rules_out.why: 10 is how many fit inside the frame, not how many are left over.
13 is every counter on the mat, and 10 of them are in the frame.
Adding makes more counters than there are. There are only 13 on the mat.

cases.explain: A teen number is ten and some more. 13 is the 10 that fills the frame and 3 more outside it, which is the whole idea behind every teen number.

given: The box says there are 13 counters.
10 counters fill the ten-frame.
2 counters rolled under the mat.
You can see 1 counter outside the frame.
debate.question: How many counters are outside the frame?

arguments.why: The box says 13 and 10 are in the frame, so 3 are outside it — and 2 of those 3 are under the mat.
Only 1 counter can be seen outside the frame. The ones under the mat are not on the mat at all.

debate.note: Both children are counting carefully; they disagree about whether a counter you cannot see still counts. Ask what the box tells you that your eyes do not.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Pencils
given: The red pencil is 8 cubes long.
The blue pencil is 5 cubes long.
All the cubes are the same size.
Both pencils were lined up at the same starting line.
cases.question: How many cubes longer is the red pencil?

rules_out.why: 8 is how long the red pencil is, not how much longer it is than the blue one.
5 is how long the blue pencil is. The question asks for the difference between them.
Adding the two lengths makes one long pencil. Comparing takes one away from the other.

cases.explain: Line them up at the same end and look at the gap. The red pencil runs 8 cubes and the blue one stops at 5, so the gap is 3 cubes.

given: The red pencil measures 8 cubes.
The blue pencil measures 5 cubes.
The blue pencil was not lined up at the starting line — it began one cube past it.
All the cubes are the same size.
debate.question: How much longer is the red pencil? Say what you measured.

arguments.why: The numbers on the page are 8 and 5, and 8 take away 5 is 3 cubes of difference.
Blue started a cube late, so it is really 6 cubes long and the gap is only 2.

debate.note: This is the whole of early measurement in one argument: a number only means a length if you started at the end of the thing. Line them up again in front of the class.

cases.title: The Case of the Triangle Standing on Its Point
given: There are 5 shapes on the mat.
3 of them have exactly 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
1 of those 3 is turned so a corner points down.
The other 2 shapes are a square and a circle.
cases.question: How many triangles are on the mat?

rules_out.why: A triangle turned on its point is still a triangle. It still has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
5 counts every shape on the mat, and a square and a circle are not triangles.

cases.explain: A shape is a triangle because of what it has, not how it sits: 3 straight sides and 3 corners. Turning one upside down changes nothing, so all 3 count.

given: There are 5 shapes on the mat.
3 of them have 3 straight sides.
On 1 of those 3 there is a small gap where two sides should meet.
The other 2 shapes are a square and a circle.
debate.question: How many triangles are on the mat?

arguments.why: It has 3 straight sides and it was drawn to be a triangle. The gap is how the pen slipped, not what the shape is.
A triangle is closed all the way round. A shape with a gap is a path, and you could walk out of it.

debate.note: Children sort this one out faster than adults expect. The question underneath it is what a shape is: what somebody meant to draw, or what is actually on the paper.

cases.title: The Case of the Book Box
given: On Monday the box held 15 books.
On Tuesday the class took out 6 books.
On Wednesday 4 books were put back.
Nobody else opened the box.
cases.question: How many books are in the box now?

rules_out.why: 9 is where the box was on Tuesday night. On Wednesday 4 books came back.
Adding all three numbers counts the books that left as if they had arrived.
The 4 books on Wednesday went in, so they are added, not taken away.

cases.explain: Walk the days in order: 15, take 6 away to get 9, put 4 back to get 13. The order of the days tells you which way each number goes.

given: On Monday the box held 15 books.
On Tuesday the class took out 6 books.
On Wednesday 4 books were put back.
Two of the books put back came from the library, not from this box.
debate.question: How many of the box's own books are in the box now?

arguments.why: Count what is in the box, whoever owns it. Four books went in: 15 take away 6, add 4, is 13.
The question asks for the box's own books. Only 2 of the 4 belong here: 15 take away 6, add 2, is 11.
None of the 6 that left has come back. The books put back are different books, so the box's own count is 15 take away 6, which is 9.

debate.note: The argument is about what the question is counting: books in the box, or books that belong to the box. Both readings are honest, and saying which one you chose is the mathematics.

cases.title: The Case of the Bundled Straws
given: Mia has 4 sticks of straws.
Every stick holds exactly 10 straws.
She also has 7 loose straws.
No straws are missing.
cases.question: How many straws does Mia have altogether?

rules_out.why: 11 adds the sticks to the loose straws as if a stick were one straw. A stick is worth 10.
74 is 7 sticks and 4 loose. Mia has it the other way round: 4 sticks and 7 loose.
28 multiplies the sticks by the loose straws, which counts neither the sticks nor the loose ones.

cases.explain: Four sticks of ten is 40 straws, and the 7 loose ones sit in the ones place: 47. The 4 and the 7 in 47 are the sticks and the loose straws, in that order.

given: Mia has 4 sticks of straws and 7 loose ones.
Every full stick holds exactly 10 straws.
One of the sticks has come undone on the table.
Mia has not counted the undone one yet.
debate.question: How many straws does Mia have? Say what you counted.

arguments.why: A stick coming undone does not lose any straws. All 4 tens and the 7 ones are still on the table: 47.
Only 3 sticks are still bundled, and she has not counted the loose pile from the fourth. What she can count in tens is 30, plus the 7: 37.

debate.note: Tens are a way of holding numbers, not a property of the straws. A child who says 37 has noticed something real — the tens got harder to see — and the move is to ask whether anything left the table.

cases.title: The Case of the Lesson That Ends Late
given: The lesson starts at 9:00.
The lesson lasts 30 minutes.
The minute hand starts pointing straight up.
Nothing interrupts the lesson.
cases.question: How many minutes past 9 does the lesson end?

rules_out.why: 60 minutes is a whole hour. The lesson is 30 minutes, which is half of one.
30 minutes is thirty, not three. The minute hand goes all the way round to the 6.

cases.explain: Thirty minutes is half a turn of the minute hand: it starts straight up at the 12 and finishes straight down at the 6. That is half past 9.

given: The lesson starts at 9:00.
The lesson lasts 30 minutes.
The teacher spent 5 minutes settling the class before starting.
The clock on the wall runs 2 minutes fast.
debate.question: What will the wall clock say when the lesson ends? Minutes past 9.

arguments.why: The lesson is 30 minutes long and it started at 9:00, so it ends at half past. The settling happened before it started.
The class was in the room from 9:00 and the settling was part of it, so 5 and 30 make 35 minutes gone.
The question asks what the wall clock will say, and the wall clock is 2 minutes ahead of the real time of 35 past.

debate.note: Three right answers to three different questions: how long the lesson was, how long the class was in the room, and what one particular clock will show. Make them say which question they answered.

cases.title: The Case of the Half Sandwich
given: The sandwich is cut into 4 pieces.
All 4 pieces are exactly the same size.
2 halves make up the whole sandwich.
Sam wants exactly half of it.
cases.question: How many pieces should Sam take?

rules_out.why: One of 4 equal pieces is a quarter of the sandwich, which is less than half.
Three pieces is more than half. The other half would only have one piece in it.
Four pieces is the whole sandwich, and Sam asked for half of it.

cases.explain: Half means the sandwich split into 2 equal shares. Four equal pieces share out 2 and 2, so half the sandwich is 2 pieces.

given: The sandwich is cut into 4 pieces.
Two of the pieces are visibly bigger than the other two.
2 halves make up the whole sandwich.
Sam wants exactly half.
debate.question: Can Sam take whole pieces and get exactly half? How many?

arguments.why: Take one big piece and one small piece. The other half is the matching big one and small one, so the two shares are the same.
Nobody said the two big pieces match each other, or that the small ones do. Without that, no two pieces are certainly half.

debate.note: The first answer is right if the pieces pair up and wrong if they do not, and the problem never says. Ask what they would need to measure to be sure — that question is the lesson.

cases.title: The Case of the Change That Felt Wrong
given: Sam pays with 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 4 pennies.
The book costs 84 cents.
A quarter is 25 cents, a dime is 10 cents, a penny is 1 cent.
Sam gets his change in pennies.
cases.question: How many pennies of change should Sam get?

rules_out.why: 99 cents is what Sam handed over. The price of the book still has to come off it.
9 counts the coins. The line of values says what each coin is worth, and a quarter is not worth the same as a penny.
84 cents is the price of the book, not the change from it.

cases.explain: Turn the coins into cents first: 75 and 20 and 4 make 99. The change is what is left once the price comes off: 99 take away 84 is 15 pennies.

given: Sam pays with 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 4 pennies.
The sign under the book says 84 cents.
The till rings it up at 79 cents.
A quarter is 25 cents, a dime is 10 cents, a penny is 1 cent.
debate.question: How much change should Sam get? Say which number you trusted, and why.

arguments.why: The sign is the price the shop put on the book: 99 take away 84 is 15.
The till is the price the shop is charging now: 99 take away 79 is 20.

debate.note: Both children can do the subtraction. What they are arguing about is which number is the price, and that is an argument shops have with customers every day.

cases.title: The Case of the Shelf That Kept Changing
given: There were 24 books on the shelf.
The class took 9 of them away to read.
Later, 5 books were put back.
Then 6 new books arrived from the library.
cases.question: How many books are on the shelf now?

rules_out.why: 20 is the shelf after the books came back but before the new ones arrived. There is one more step.
15 stops after the class took books away, and 5 of those came back afterwards.
44 adds every number in the problem, which counts the 9 that left as if they had arrived.

cases.explain: Take the events in the order they happened: 24, take 9 to get 15, put 5 back to get 20, add 6 new to get 26. The order of the sentences tells you which way each number goes.

given: There were 24 books on the shelf.
The class took 9 of them away to read.
Later, 5 books were put back.
6 new books arrived but are still in their box by the door.
debate.question: How many books are on the shelf?

arguments.why: The 6 new books belong to this shelf and have arrived in the room. Counting what the class now has gives 26.
The question asks about the shelf, and the new books are in a box by the door. On the shelf there are 20.

debate.note: Every child here can do the arithmetic. What they are deciding is where the shelf ends, and that is a reading question wearing a maths hat.

cases.title: The Case of the Marble Jar
given: The jar held 62 marbles this morning.
Leo took out 28 of them.
Later he put 15 marbles back in.
Nobody else went near the jar.
cases.question: How many marbles are in the jar now?

rules_out.why: 34 is the jar after Leo took marbles out. He put 15 back in afterwards.
19 takes the 15 away as well. They went into the jar, so they are added.
105 adds all three numbers, which treats the 28 that left as if they had arrived.

cases.explain: Work the jar forward in time: 62, take 28 away to get 34, put 15 back to get 49. Each sentence either adds to the jar or takes from it, and the words say which.

given: The jar held 62 marbles this morning.
Leo took out 28 of them.
Later he put 15 marbles back in.
4 of the marbles he put back came from a different jar.
debate.question: How many of this jar's own marbles are in it now?

arguments.why: Count what is in the jar. Forty-nine marbles are in there, and a marble does not change jars by being moved.
The question says this jar's own marbles, and 4 of the 49 belong somewhere else: 49 take away 4 is 45.

debate.note: Same jar, same arithmetic, two readings of the question. Read the question aloud twice and ask which of the two it is asking.

cases.title: The Case of the Matching Shaded Parts
given: Ana's rectangle is split into 3 equal parts and she shades 2 of them.
Ben's rectangle is exactly the same size as Ana's.
Ben's rectangle is split into 6 equal parts.
They want the same amount of their rectangle shaded.
cases.question: How many of Ben's parts should he shade?

rules_out.why: 2 of Ben's parts is the same number of parts, but his parts are half the size of Ana's, so it is half as much paper.
3 of Ben's 6 parts is half the rectangle, and Ana shaded 2 of 3, which is more than half.
6 parts is Ben's whole rectangle, and Ana left one of her three parts unshaded.

cases.explain: The rectangles are the same size, so each of Ana's thirds covers two of Ben's sixths. Two thirds is therefore four sixths, and Ben shades 4.

given: Ana's rectangle is split into 3 equal parts and she shades 2 of them.
Ben's rectangle is split into 6 equal parts.
Ben's rectangle is twice as long as Ana's.
They want the same amount of paper covered.
debate.question: How many of Ben's parts should he shade? Say what you matched.

arguments.why: To shade the same fraction of his own rectangle, Ben needs two thirds of it, and two thirds of six parts is four.
Ben's rectangle is twice as big, so each of his sixths is exactly the size of one of Ana's thirds. Two of them cover the same paper she did.

debate.note: Two thirds of a bigger rectangle is more paper than two thirds of a smaller one. This is the first time a fraction stops meaning anything until you say what it is a fraction of, and it is worth slowing down on.

cases.title: The Case of the Short Tray
given: The class baked 6 trays of cookies.
A full tray holds 4 cookies.
One tray came out of the oven with 1 cookie missing.
Nobody ate any.
cases.question: How many cookies did the class bake?

rules_out.why: 24 is six full trays, and one of the trays was not full.
Adding the trays to the cookies-per-tray counts neither of them. Four cookies on each of six trays is a multiplication.
A missing cookie comes off the total, not on.

cases.explain: Equal groups first: six fours is 24. Then the one line that breaks the pattern: a cookie is missing, so 23.

given: The class baked 6 trays of cookies.
A full tray holds 4 cookies.
Two trays came out with gaps in them.
Nobody counted the gaps.
debate.question: How many cookies did the class bake? Give a number you can defend.

arguments.why: Six trays of four is 24. The gaps were never counted, so there is no number to take away.
A gap is at least one cookie and two trays have gaps, so 24 take away 2 is the most we can still claim.
If a tray with gaps cannot be counted at all, only the four full trays count: four fours is 16.

debate.note: This is the difference between a number and an estimate. 24 is the most there can be, 16 the least, and the honest answer says which of the two it is.

cases.title: The Case of the Tins That Kept Moving
given: The school had collected 428 tins by Monday night.
On Tuesday another 156 tins came in.
On Wednesday 90 tins were sent to the food bank.
No other tins moved all week.
cases.question: How many tins does the school have now?

rules_out.why: 584 is where the collection stood on Tuesday night, before 90 tins left on Wednesday.
674 adds all three numbers, which counts the 90 tins that left as though they had arrived.
362 takes Tuesday's tins away instead of adding them. More tins coming in makes the pile bigger.

cases.explain: Take the week in order: 428, add Tuesday's 156 to reach 584, then take away the 90 that left on Wednesday to reach 494. Each sentence says whether the pile grew or shrank.

given: The school had collected 428 tins by Monday night.
On Tuesday another 156 tins came in.
On Wednesday 90 tins were sent to the food bank.
12 of the tins are past their date and the food bank will not take them.
debate.question: How many tins does the school have to give? Defend the number.

arguments.why: Count the tins in the room: 428 and 156 in, 90 out, leaves 494 tins on the shelves.
The question is what the school has to give, and 12 of them cannot be given: 494 take away 12 is 482.

debate.note: The arithmetic is finished before the argument starts. What is in dispute is whether a tin nobody will accept is still a tin you have, which is the sort of thing a food drive actually has to decide.

cases.title: The Case of the Broken Bar
given: The chocolate bar is broken into 8 equal pieces.
Jo eats 3 of the pieces.
All 8 pieces are exactly the same size.
Nobody else eats any.
cases.question: What fraction of the bar is left?

rules_out.why: 3/8 is the part Jo ate. The question asks what is still there.
5 is how many pieces are left, but a fraction says how many out of how many: 5 out of 8.
1/8 is a single piece. Five pieces are left, not one.

cases.explain: The bottom number is how many equal pieces the whole was broken into, and the top is how many you have. Eight pieces, three eaten, five left: 5/8.

given: The chocolate bar is broken into 8 pieces.
Jo eats 3 of the pieces.
Two of the pieces broke badly and are much smaller than the others.
Nobody else eats any.
debate.question: How much of the bar is left? Defend your fraction.

arguments.why: Count the pieces: 8 pieces, 3 gone, 5 left. Five out of eight pieces is 5/8.
If the two small pieces were among the three Jo ate, far more chocolate is left than 5/8 — nearer three quarters of the bar.

debate.note: A fraction needs equal parts, and this bar has not got them. The honest answer is that 5/8 counts pieces and nobody has said what fraction of the chocolate that is — which is exactly the thing the word equal is doing in the definition.

cases.title: The Case of the Fence and the Wall
given: The garden bed is 7 feet long.
The garden bed is 4 feet wide.
A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.
The fence must go all the way round the bed.
cases.question: How many feet of fence are needed?

rules_out.why: 28 is 7 times 4, which is the ground inside the bed. A fence runs along the edge, not across the middle.
11 is one long side and one short side. There are two of each.
14 is the two long sides only, and the fence has to turn the corners and come back along the short ones.

cases.explain: Walk the edge and add what you walk: 7 and 4 and 7 and 4 is 22 feet. Perimeter is the walk round the outside; area is the ground inside, and they are not the same question.

given: The garden bed is 7 feet by 4 feet.
A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.
One of the 7-foot sides runs flat against a wall.
The gardener wants to be able to reach the bed from every side.
debate.question: How many feet of fence should they buy? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The wall is already a fence on that side, so only the other three sides need fencing: 7 and 4 and 4 is 15 feet.
Reaching the bed from every side means pulling it off the wall, and then all four sides are open: the full 22 feet.

debate.note: Perimeter is a measurement, but how much fence to buy is a decision. Ask which of the two sentences in the problem the gardener meant to be the important one.

cases.title: The Case of the Square That Is Also Something Else
given: There are 6 shapes on the board.
4 of them have 4 straight sides and are closed all the way round.
Of those 4, two also have all their sides the same length.
The other 2 shapes are a triangle and a circle.
cases.question: How many of the shapes are quadrilaterals?

rules_out.why: 2 is how many are squares. A square is a kind of quadrilateral, so the other two four-sided shapes count as well.
6 counts every shape on the board, and a triangle and a circle do not have four straight sides.

cases.explain: A quadrilateral is any closed shape with four straight sides, and that is the whole test. The squares pass it too: being a square is a way of being a quadrilateral, not an alternative to it.

given: There are 6 shapes on the board.
4 of them look like they have 4 straight sides.
On one of those 4, a side bows out very slightly.
The other 2 shapes are a triangle and a circle.
debate.question: How many quadrilaterals are on the board? Say what your test is.

arguments.why: It was drawn to be a four-sided shape and everyone can see which four sides are meant. A wobble in the pen is not a property of the shape.
A quadrilateral has four straight sides, and a side that bows is not straight. If we let that one in, the word stops meaning anything.

debate.note: Definitions in geometry are exact, and the drawings in front of children never are. Both answers are defensible; what is not defensible is refusing to say which test you used.

cases.title: The Case of the Shared Ribbon
given: The roll held 3 metres of ribbon.
Mia used 3/4 of a metre.
Jo used 1 1/2 metres.
Nothing else was cut from the roll.
cases.question: How many metres of ribbon are left?

rules_out.why: Only Mia's piece has come off. Jo cut some too.
Only Jo's piece has come off. Mia cut 3/4 of a metre as well.
1 1/2 is one and a half, not one. The extra half metre is still missing from the subtraction.

cases.explain: Put everything over the same denominator: 3 metres is 12/4, Mia took 3/4, Jo took 6/4. 12/4 minus 3/4 minus 6/4 leaves 3/4 of a metre.

given: The roll held 3 metres of ribbon.
Mia used 3/4 of a metre.
Jo used about one and a half metres.
The scraps under the table come to 1/4 of a metre altogether.
debate.question: How much usable ribbon is left? Defend your number.

arguments.why: Take off what was used: 3 minus 3/4 minus 1 1/2 leaves 3/4 of a metre on the roll.
Scraps are not usable length, so they come off too: 3/4 minus 1/4 is 1/2 a metre.
'About one and a half' could be a little under, and a 1/4 metre of scraps still cuts short pieces, so close to a metre is defensible.

debate.note: The word 'about' is doing the work here. Ask which numbers in the problem are exact and which one is a measurement, because only one of them can be argued with.

cases.title: The Case of the Children Left Standing
given: There are 7 tables in the hall.
Each table seats 6 children.
50 children are coming.
Every child needs a seat.
cases.question: How many children will have nowhere to sit?

rules_out.why: 42 is how many seats there are, not how many children are left over once they are filled.
50 is every child coming, and 42 of them do get a seat.
2 is how many extra tables would be needed. That is a useful number, but it answers a different question.

cases.explain: Two steps, in order. Seven tables of six is 42 seats, and 50 children arrive, so 8 children are left standing. The second step is the one the question actually asks about.

given: There are 7 tables in the hall.
Each table seats 6 children.
2 of the tables have been pushed to the side to hold the food.
50 children are coming and every child needs a seat.
debate.question: How many children will have nowhere to sit?

arguments.why: There are 7 tables in the hall and they seat 6 each, so there are 42 seats in the room and 8 children over.
Only 5 tables are free to sit at, which is 30 seats, so 20 children have nowhere to go.

debate.note: Both answers come from the same multiplication done carefully. The disagreement is over what counts as a seat, and the food tables are the whole of it.

cases.title: The Case of the Crayon Order
given: A box holds 24 crayons.
The school orders 36 boxes.
Every box leaves the factory full.
None of the crayons are broken.
cases.question: How many crayons did the school order?

rules_out.why: 624 multiplies the tens together and the ones together and stops. It leaves out 20 sixes and 4 thirties.
144 is 24 times 6, which is six boxes. The order is for thirty-six.
60 adds the two numbers. Thirty-six boxes of twenty-four is a multiplication, not a sum.

cases.explain: Break 36 into 30 and 6: 24 thirties is 720 and 24 sixes is 144, and together that is 864. Every partial product has to be counted, which is what the 624 answer forgets.

given: A box holds 24 crayons.
The school ordered 36 boxes.
4 of the boxes arrived already opened and short.
Nobody counted what was missing from those 4.
debate.question: How many crayons did the school get? Give a number you can defend.

arguments.why: Thirty-six boxes of twenty-four is 864, and nobody has said a single crayon is actually missing — only that the boxes were open.
Only 32 boxes can be trusted to be full: 32 times 24 is 768, and that is the most the school can claim.

debate.note: 864 is what was ordered and 768 is what can be proved. When they differ, the useful thing is to say which one you are writing on the form and why.

cases.title: The Case of the Tape Round the Rug
given: The classroom rug is 9 feet long and 6 feet wide.
A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.
Tape runs all the way round the edge of the rug.
Tape is sold by the foot.
cases.question: How many feet of tape are needed?

rules_out.why: 54 is 9 times 6, the floor the rug covers. Tape goes round the edge, not across the rug.
18 is the two long sides only. The tape has to come back along the two short ones as well.
15 is one long side and one short side — half of the way round.

cases.explain: Trace the edge with a finger and add as you go: 9, 6, 9, 6. That is 30 feet. Area would be the carpet itself; this is the piping round it.

given: The rug is 9 feet by 6 feet.
A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.
The tape has to overlap itself by 1 foot where the two ends meet.
Tape is sold only in whole feet.
debate.question: How many feet of tape should they buy?

arguments.why: The distance round the rug is 30 feet, and that is what the tape has to cover.
A foot of it is spent on the overlap and covers nothing new, so 30 feet of tape leaves a foot of rug bare. Buy 31.

debate.note: The perimeter is 30 and the answer to the shopping question is 31. Worth naming out loud: the measurement and the amount to buy are different numbers, and the overlap is the reason.

cases.title: The Case of the Folded Shapes
given: There are 3 shapes on the table: a square, a rectangle that is not a square, and a triangle.
A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines of symmetry.
The triangle has 0 lines of symmetry.
cases.question: How many lines of symmetry are there altogether?

rules_out.why: 3 is how many shapes are on the table, not how many fold lines they have between them.
4 is the square's lines on their own. The rectangle has some too.
2 is the rectangle's lines on their own, and the square has four more.

cases.explain: A line of symmetry is a fold that lands the shape exactly on itself. Count each shape's folds and add them: 4 and 2 and none at all is 6.

given: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines of symmetry.
The third shape is a triangle whose two longer sides look equal but have not been measured.
A triangle with two equal sides has 1 line of symmetry.
debate.question: How many lines of symmetry are there altogether? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The two sides look equal, and a triangle with two equal sides folds onto itself once: 4 and 2 and 1 is 7.
Nobody has measured those sides. Until somebody does, the triangle cannot be claimed to fold, so only the 4 and the 2 can be counted.

debate.note: Fold the triangle and the argument ends in four seconds, which is the point: symmetry is a claim you can test, and looking is not testing. Have the paper ready.

cases.title: The Case of the Receipt That Rang Twice
given: The receipt lists milk at 3.49, bread at 2.75 and eggs at 4.20.
The total printed at the bottom is 13.19.
The shop charges no tax on food.
Exactly one item was scanned twice.
cases.question: Which item was scanned twice? Give its price in dollars.

rules_out.why: Milk twice would make the total 13.93, and the receipt says 13.19.
Eggs twice would make the total 14.64, and the receipt says 13.19.
10.44 is what the three items come to once each, which is what the receipt should have printed, not what it did print.

cases.explain: Add the three listed prices: 10.44. The receipt took 13.19, so the overcharge is 13.19 minus 10.44, which is 2.75 — and 2.75 is the bread.

given: The receipt lists milk at 3.49, bread at 2.75 and eggs at 4.20.
The total printed is 13.19.
There are two loaves of bread in the bag.
The shop adds a 2.75 crate charge to delivery orders, and this was a delivery.
debate.question: How much, if anything, should the shop refund? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The three listed prices come to 10.44. The receipt took 2.75 more than it lists, and a charge that is not printed should come back.
The 2.75 is the crate charge on a delivery. The total is right; the receipt simply does not print that line.
If the 2.75 is the crate, then the second loaf in the bag has not been paid for at all, and the customer owes 2.75 rather than being owed it.

debate.note: Every one of these is arithmetic a fifth grader can do. What they are arguing about is which story the numbers are evidence for, which is the whole of modelling.

cases.title: The Case of the Sign With No Brackets
given: The expression is 4 + 3 × 6.
There are no brackets anywhere in it.
Multiplication is done before addition.
Every number in it is a whole number.
cases.question: What does the expression equal?

rules_out.why: 42 is what you get working strictly left to right, which is (4 + 3) × 6. There are no brackets to make that happen.
18 is 3 times 6 on its own, and the 4 is still in the expression.
13 adds all three numbers, treating the times sign as a plus.

cases.explain: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so 3 × 6 is a single quantity of 18 and the 4 is added to it: 22. Brackets exist precisely to overrule that when you want (4 + 3) × 6.

given: A sign at the fair reads: 4 + 3 × 6 free tickets.
There are no brackets anywhere on the sign.
The manager says she meant 4 tickets, and then 3 groups of 6 more.
A customer read it left to right and worked out 42.
debate.question: How many tickets does the sign promise? Defend it.

arguments.why: Written without brackets, the expression means 4 + 18. That is the convention every reader of mathematics is entitled to assume, and it is what the manager meant.
A sign is read by ordinary people left to right. The shop wrote something ambiguous in public, and the customer's reading is a reasonable one.

debate.note: The mathematics has one answer and the argument is about who carries the cost of an ambiguous sign. Both are worth having: convention is what makes writing maths possible, and it only works when the reader knows it.

cases.title: The Case of the Flour That Is Not Enough Yet
given: The recipe needs 3/4 of a cup of flour.
Sam has already put in 1/3 of a cup.
The cup is the same size every time.
Nothing else has gone into the bowl.
cases.question: How much more flour does Sam need, in cups?

rules_out.why: 2 comes from taking the tops and the bottoms away separately. It would mean Sam needs more than the recipe asks for in total.
13/12 adds the two amounts instead of comparing them. That is more than a whole cup, and the recipe only wants 3/4.
1/4 is what is left of a cup after 3/4. Sam has put in 1/3, not 3/4.

cases.explain: Twelfths hold both: 3/4 is 9/12 and 1/3 is 4/12. The gap between them is 5/12 of a cup. A common denominator is just a unit both amounts can be counted in.

given: The recipe needs 3/4 of a cup of flour.
Sam has already put in 1/3 of a cup.
Sam's measuring cup is marked only in quarters.
Nothing else has gone into the bowl.
debate.question: How much more flour should Sam add? Say what you would do at the counter.

arguments.why: The exact shortfall is 9/12 minus 4/12, which is 5/12 of a cup, and that is the honest answer to what is missing.
There is no 5/12 mark on the cup. Half is the nearest mark and it is closer to 5/12 than a quarter is, so half is what actually gets added.

debate.note: 5/12 is right and unmeasurable with the equipment in the room. Ask which is the better answer for a person holding the cup, and whether being slightly over matters in bread.

cases.title: The Case of the Box That Holds Less Than It Measures
given: The box is 6 inches long, 4 inches wide and 3 inches tall.
The cubes are 1 inch on every side.
The box is a rectangular box with square corners.
The cubes are packed in with no gaps.
cases.question: How many cubes fit in the box?

rules_out.why: 24 is one layer on the bottom, 6 by 4. The box is 3 inches tall, so three layers go in.
13 adds the three measurements. Volume is how many cubes fill the space, which is a multiplication.
108 is the area of the outside of the box. That is what you would wrap it in, not what goes inside.

cases.explain: Build it in layers. The bottom holds 6 by 4, which is 24 cubes, and the box is 3 inches tall, so three of those layers stack: 72 cubes.

given: The box measures 6 inches by 4 inches by 3 inches on the outside.
The cubes are 1 inch on every side.
There is a padded lining 1 inch thick across the bottom of the box.
The cubes have to sit flat.
debate.question: How many cubes actually fit? Say what you measured.

arguments.why: Six by four by three is 72, and those are the measurements the problem gives for the box.
The lining eats an inch of the height, so only two layers of cubes fit above it: 6 by 4 by 2 is 48.

debate.note: The volume formula is not in dispute; which height to put into it is. Outside measurements and inside space are different numbers for any box with a wall, which is every real box.

cases.title: The Case of the Rectangle in the Textbook
given: There are 5 quadrilaterals on the board.
3 of them have 4 right angles.
2 of those 3 also have 4 equal sides.
The other 2 shapes have no right angles at all.
cases.question: How many of the shapes are rectangles?

rules_out.why: 1 counts only the shape that is a rectangle and not a square. The two squares have 4 right angles too, so they are rectangles as well.
5 counts every quadrilateral on the board, and 2 of them have no right angles.

cases.explain: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles, and that is the entire definition. A square passes it and adds a condition of its own, so every square is a rectangle — the categories sit inside one another rather than beside one another.

given: There are 5 quadrilaterals on the board.
3 of them have 4 right angles.
2 of those 3 also have 4 equal sides.
In the class textbook, the picture labelled 'rectangle' is always a long shape and never a square.
debate.question: How many rectangles are on the board? Say which meaning you used.

arguments.why: By the definition, four right angles makes a rectangle. The squares have four right angles, so all 3 count.
Every picture the class has been shown of a rectangle is a long shape. In the way this room has used the word, a square is not one of them.

debate.note: This is where a lot of children quietly lose geometry: the textbook teaches by picture and the definition says something wider. Say plainly that the definition wins, and that the pictures have been misleading them.

cases.title: The Case of the Better Buy
given: The small box holds 12 ounces and costs 3.60.
The large box holds 20 ounces and costs 5.40.
Both boxes hold exactly the same cereal.
Neither box is on special offer.
cases.question: What is the price per ounce of the better buy, in dollars?

rules_out.why: 0.30 is the small box's rate, and it is the higher of the two.
0.225 is the price of the extra ounces only — 1.80 more for 8 more ounces — not the price per ounce of a box.
1.80 is how much more the large box costs altogether. It is a difference, not a rate.

cases.explain: A rate is price divided by amount. 3.60 over 12 ounces is 0.30 an ounce; 5.40 over 20 ounces is 0.27 an ounce. Lower is better, so the large box.

given: The small box holds 12 ounces and costs 3.60.
The large box holds 20 ounces and costs 5.40.
This family eats a box a week and throws out about 4 ounces of a large box gone stale.
There is shelf room for one box at a time.
debate.question: Which box is the better buy for this family? Give the rate you are using.

options.label: 0.3375 an ounce eaten, the large box

arguments.why: Per ounce bought, the large box is cheaper: 5.40 over 20 is 0.27.
Per ounce eaten, the large box is 5.40 over 16, which is 0.3375 — worse than the small box.
If the waste is real, the small box at 0.30 an ounce with nothing thrown away is the better buy.

debate.note: Nobody is disputing the arithmetic; they are disputing the denominator. Ask each student what they divided by, and why that is the right amount to divide by.

cases.title: The Case of the Ribbon That Comes Out Exact
given: The ribbon is 3/4 of a metre long.
Each bow uses 1/8 of a metre.
No ribbon is wasted.
Only whole bows count.
cases.question: How many bows can be made?

rules_out.why: 8 eighths make a whole metre, and there is only 3/4 of a metre of ribbon on the roll.
Multiplying the two fractions makes a smaller piece. Dividing is what asks how many of the small pieces fit inside the big one.

cases.explain: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of it fit. An eighth fits into a whole metre eight times, and into three quarters of a metre six times, so six bows.

given: The ribbon is 3/4 of a metre, which is 75 centimetres.
Each bow uses 1/8 of a metre, which is 12.5 centimetres.
Every knot wastes about 1 centimetre of ribbon.
Only whole bows count.
debate.question: How many bows can actually be made? Defend the number.

arguments.why: Three quarters divided by an eighth is exactly 6. The division is not in question and it comes out whole.
Six bows need all 75 centimetres with nothing spare, and six knots eat 6 more. There is not enough ribbon for the sixth.

debate.note: An answer that divides exactly is the one to be most careful with: it has used every millimetre and left no room for the thing the problem did not mention. Ask what would have to be true for 6 to work.

cases.title: The Case of the Ticket Price
given: The school spent 210 dollars in total.
They bought 14 tickets.
Every ticket cost the same.
There was no delivery charge and no fee.
cases.question: What did one ticket cost, in dollars?

rules_out.why: 196 takes 14 away from 210. The 14 is a count of tickets, not an amount of money to subtract.
224 adds them, which would make one ticket cost more than the whole order.
2940 multiplies them. The total is already known; the job is to share it out.

cases.explain: Fourteen equal prices make 210, so one of them is 210 shared into 14 parts: 15 dollars. In symbols that is 14t = 210, and dividing both sides by 14 is the same move.

given: The school paid 210 dollars in total.
They bought 14 tickets.
The order also included a 14-dollar booking fee.
Every ticket cost the same as every other.
debate.question: What did one ticket cost? Say what you divided.

arguments.why: 210 dollars left the school's account for 14 tickets, so each ticket cost the school 15 dollars all in.
The fee is not part of a ticket's price. Take it off first: 196 for 14 tickets is 14 dollars each.

debate.note: The equation is the same either way; what changes is whether the fee belongs inside it. Ask which number the school would put on a reimbursement form, and why.

cases.title: The Case of the Slanted Height
given: The triangle has a base of 12 cm.
Its height is 5 cm.
The area of a triangle is the base times the height, divided by 2.
Both measurements are exact.
cases.question: What is the area, in square centimetres?

rules_out.why: 60 is base times height and stops there. A triangle is half the rectangle that would box it in.
17 adds the base to the height. Area is a product, not a sum.
120 doubles instead of halving, which makes a shape four times the size of the triangle.

cases.explain: Any triangle is exactly half of the rectangle built on its base and height. 12 by 5 is 60, and the triangle is half of that: 30 square centimetres.

given: The triangle has a base of 12 cm.
A side of it was measured as 5 cm.
Area is base times height, divided by 2.
The 5 cm was measured along a slanting side, not straight up from the base.
debate.question: What is the area? Say what you used as the height.

arguments.why: The numbers on the page are 12 and 5, and the formula takes a base and a height: 12 times 5 over 2 is 30.
A slanting side is always longer than the straight-up height, so the real height is under 5 and the area is under 30 — nearer 24 if the height is 4.

debate.note: This is the single most common error in triangle area, and it is not an arithmetic error. The height has to be perpendicular to the base, and a number labelled 5 does not tell you whether it was.

cases.title: The Case of the One High Score
given: 5 students scored 4, 6, 7, 8 and 35 on the quiz.
The quiz was out of 40.
The mean is the total divided by how many there are.
The median is the middle score once they are in order.
cases.question: What is the mean score?

rules_out.why: 7 is the median, the middle score. It is a fair summary but it is not the mean.
60 is the total of all five scores, before it is shared among the five students.
35 is the highest score one student got, not an average of the class.

cases.explain: Add the five scores to get 60, then share that total equally among the five students: 12 each. Notice that four of the five actually scored below it.

given: 5 students scored 4, 6, 7, 8 and 35 on the quiz.
The quiz was out of 40.
The mean is 12 and the median is 7.
The teacher has to report one number for how the class did.
debate.question: Which number should the teacher report? Defend it.

arguments.why: The mean uses every score, including the 35. Throwing away a real result because it is inconvenient is how reporting goes wrong.
Four of the five students scored 8 or less. A number that sits above almost everyone describes nobody in the room.

debate.note: Both numbers are correctly calculated and they tell different stories about the same five children. The useful habit is reporting both and saying what the gap between them means.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Discounts
given: The jacket is marked 80 dollars.
The sign says 25 percent off.
A coupon takes 10 dollars off at the till.
The store takes the percentage off first, then the coupon.
cases.question: What does the jacket cost at the till, in dollars?

rules_out.why: 52.50 is the coupon taken off first and the 25 percent off what was left. The store does it the other way round.
60 is the sale price before the coupon is handed over.
45 treats 25 percent as 25 dollars. A percentage is of something, and 25 percent of 80 is 20.

cases.explain: 25 percent of 80 is 20, so the sale price is 60. The coupon is a flat 10 off that, giving 50. Order matters here: coupon first would have given 52.50.

given: The jacket is marked 80 dollars.
The sign says 25 percent off.
A coupon takes 10 dollars off.
The coupon is printed 'cannot be combined with other offers'.
debate.question: What should the customer pay? Defend it.

arguments.why: Nothing in the arithmetic stops both: 60, then 10 off, is 50. 'Other offers' may well mean other coupons rather than the store's own sale.
The coupon cannot be combined, so the customer takes whichever is better. 25 percent off is 60, and that beats the coupon.
If the customer hands over the coupon, that is the offer they chose: 80 minus 10 is 70. It is the worse deal, but it is what the rule allows.

debate.note: All three are computed correctly. The disagreement is over what one sentence in the problem means, which is exactly the argument a shop has with a customer.

cases.title: The Case of the Thermometer in the Sun
given: The temperature at dawn was -6 degrees.
It rose 14 degrees by noon.
It fell 9 degrees again by midnight.
Nothing else changed it.
cases.question: What was the temperature at midnight, in degrees?

rules_out.why: 8 degrees is noon, before the temperature fell again in the evening.
11 comes from starting at 6 instead of -6. Dawn was below zero, and that minus sign changes every step after it.
-29 takes the 14 away as well. The temperature rose by 14, so it is added.

cases.explain: Walk it along a number line: start at -6, go up 14 to reach 8, then down 9 to land on -1. Rising is adding and falling is subtracting, whatever side of zero you are on.

given: The dawn reading was -6 degrees.
It rose 14 degrees by noon.
It fell 9 degrees again by midnight.
The thermometer reads 2 degrees too warm in sunlight, and the dawn reading was taken in the sun.
debate.question: What was the temperature at midnight? Defend it.

arguments.why: The three readings are the data we have, and working them through gives -1. Correcting a reading means guessing at a number nobody took.
Dawn was really -8, not -6, because the sun was on the thermometer. Every step after it shifts by the same 2 degrees, so midnight is -3.

debate.note: A known, consistent instrument error is the one kind of correction you can make with confidence, and it moves every later number by the same amount. Ask what would change if the error were only sometimes there.

cases.title: The Case of the Fare With Something Extra In It
given: The taxi charges a flat fee of 3 dollars.
It then charges 2 dollars for every mile.
The ride came to 23 dollars.
There were no other charges at all.
cases.question: How many miles was the ride?

rules_out.why: 11.5 divides the whole fare by 2 and forgets the flat fee, which bought no distance at all.
13 adds the fee instead of taking it off. The fee is part of the 23 already.
20 is the number of dollars spent on mileage, not the number of miles those dollars bought.

cases.explain: Take the flat fee out of the total first, because it bought no distance: 23 minus 3 is 20 dollars of mileage. At 2 dollars a mile that is 10 miles. In symbols, 3 + 2m = 23.

given: The taxi charges 3 dollars flat and 2 dollars a mile.
The payment came to 23 dollars in total.
The passenger added a 3-dollar tip, which is inside that 23.
There were no other charges.
debate.question: How many miles was the ride? Say what you took off first.

arguments.why: Twenty-three dollars changed hands against a fare of 3 plus 2 a mile, and solving that gives 10 miles.
A tip is not a fare. Take off the 3-dollar fee and the 3-dollar tip, leaving 17 dollars of mileage: 8.5 miles.

debate.note: The equation is only as good as what you agreed to put in it. Ask which dollars the taxi company charged and which the passenger chose to add.

cases.title: The Case of the Face Nobody Sees
given: The box is a cube.
Each edge is 5 inches long.
A cube has 6 square faces.
All of the faces are the same size.
cases.question: What is the surface area, in square inches?

rules_out.why: 125 is 5 cubed, which is the space inside the box. Surface area is the skin, not the filling.
30 is 6 times 5, which counts one edge per face rather than one square face per face.
25 is a single face. There are six of them.

cases.explain: Each face is a 5 by 5 square, so each is 25 square inches, and a cube has six of them: 150 square inches. Volume would be the inside; this is the wrapping paper.

given: The box is a cube with 5-inch edges.
A cube has 6 square faces, each 25 square inches.
The bottom face sits flat on a shelf and is never seen.
The paper is being bought to make the box look good on display.
debate.question: How many square inches of paper should they buy?

arguments.why: The surface area of the box is 150 square inches, and wrapping it means covering the box, not covering the parts of it you happen to look at.
The paper is for display and the bottom is never seen, so five faces at 25 each is 125 — and the sixth face is paper in the bin.

debate.note: Surface area has one value and the amount to buy depends on the job. Both children should be able to state the surface area and then say what they are leaving off and why.

cases.title: The Case of the Counter Nobody Remembers Replacing
given: The bag holds 3 red counters and 5 blue counters.
There is nothing else in the bag.
One counter is taken out without looking.
Every counter is equally likely to be picked.
cases.question: What is the probability it is red?

rules_out.why: 3/5 compares the reds to the blues. A probability compares the reds to every counter in the bag.
5/8 is the chance of drawing blue, which is the other outcome.
1/3 would be right if there were three equally likely colours. There are 8 counters in two colours.

cases.explain: A probability is the outcomes you want over all the outcomes there are. Three counters are red out of 8 in the bag, so 3/8.

given: The bag held 3 red counters and 5 blue counters.
One counter was taken out and it was red.
Nobody can remember whether it was put back.
A second counter is about to be taken.
debate.question: What is the probability the second counter is red? Defend it.

arguments.why: If the red counter stayed out, 2 reds remain among 7 counters, so the chance has dropped to 2/7.
If it went back, the bag is exactly as it started and the second draw is the same 3/8 as the first.

debate.note: Whether a draw is replaced is not a detail, it is the whole model, and the problem has deliberately not said. The answer is that we cannot tell, and the useful work is saying what each assumption gives.

cases.title: The Case of the Identical Bills
given: Plan A charges 20 dollars a month plus 0.10 a minute.
Plan B charges 35 dollars a month and nothing per minute.
Both plans bill whole months.
Last month the two bills came to exactly the same amount.
cases.question: How many minutes were used last month?

rules_out.why: 15 is the gap between the two monthly charges in dollars. It becomes minutes only after it is divided by the per-minute rate.
350 is what 35 dollars buys at 10 cents a minute, which ignores Plan A's own 20-dollar monthly charge.
550 comes from adding the two monthly charges. The bills were equal, not combined.

cases.explain: Set the two costs equal: 20 + 0.10m = 35. The fixed charges differ by 15 dollars, and at 10 cents a minute that gap takes 150 minutes to close. Below 150 minutes Plan A is cheaper; above it, Plan B.

given: Plan A charges 20 dollars a month plus 0.10 a minute.
Plan B charges 35 dollars a month and nothing per minute.
The family used 150 minutes last month and 400 the month before.
Next month is the school holidays.
debate.question: Which plan should the family choose? Name the number of minutes your answer rests on.

arguments.why: At 150 minutes the plans cost the same, and the most recent month is the best evidence of the next one. At or below 150, Plan A wins.
The two months average 275 minutes, which is well past the 150-minute crossing point, so Plan B.
The holidays are the heavier month, and 400 minutes costs 60 dollars on Plan A against 35 on Plan B. Plan for the heavy month.

debate.note: The algebra is settled: the plans cross at 150 minutes. What is not settled is which month predicts next month, and that is a modelling choice rather than an arithmetic mistake.

cases.title: The Case of the Square That Is Not Quite Six
given: The square has an area of 40 square cm.
The side length is the number that multiplies by itself to give the area.
6 times 6 is 36.
7 times 7 is 49.
cases.question: Which whole number does the side length sit just above?

rules_out.why: 7 squared is 49, which is bigger than 40, so 7 is the number the side sits below rather than above.
20 is half of 40. Halving and square rooting are different operations and only agree at 0 and 2.
40 is the area. The side is the number whose square is 40, not 40 itself.

cases.explain: 40 sits between 36 and 49, so its square root sits between 6 and 7 — closer to 6, because 40 is closer to 36. That is how you pin down an irrational number without a calculator.

given: The square has an area of 40 square cm.
6 squared is 36 and 7 squared is 49.
6.3 squared is 39.69 and 6.4 squared is 40.96.
The square is being cut from cloth and must not come out too small.
debate.question: What side length should be used, to one decimal place?

arguments.why: 39.69 is only 0.31 away from 40 and 40.96 is 0.96 away, so 6.3 is the better approximation of the root.
Cut at 6.3 and the cloth is too small and cannot be made bigger. When an error only hurts in one direction, round the safe way.

debate.note: Nearest is the right answer to the arithmetic question and the wrong answer to the cutting question. Ask what happens if you are wrong in each direction — that decides how to round far more often than nearest does.

cases.title: The Case of the Candle That Started Slowly
given: The candle was 20 cm tall when it was lit.
After 3 hours it was 14 cm tall.
It burns at a steady rate.
It carries on burning at that same rate.
cases.question: How many centimetres does it burn each hour?

rules_out.why: 6 cm is the whole drop across three hours. A rate is the drop in one of them.
3 is the number of hours, not a number of centimetres.
14 cm is how tall the candle still is, not how much of it has gone.

cases.explain: A rate of change is the change divided by the time it took: 6 cm over 3 hours is 2 cm an hour. That 2 is the slope of the line, and the 20 it started at is the intercept.

given: The candle was 20 cm when lit and 14 cm after 3 hours.
It burns at a steady rate once it is properly going.
The first 20 minutes went on getting the wick established, with almost no wax burnt.
It carries on at the rate it reached.
debate.question: How fast is it burning now? Say what you divided by.

arguments.why: Six centimetres went in three hours, and a steady rate is the total change over the total time: 2 cm an hour.
Almost nothing burnt in the first 20 minutes, so 6 cm went in 2 hours 40, which is 2.25 cm an hour from here on.

debate.note: A straight line through two points is an average, and an average over a period that includes a slow start understates what is happening now. Ask which of the two numbers predicts the next hour better.

cases.title: The Case of the Ladder and the Window
given: The ladder is 10 feet long.
Its foot stands 6 feet out from the wall.
The wall meets the ground at a right angle, and 10 squared minus 6 squared is 64.
8 times 8 is 64.
cases.question: How high up the wall does the ladder reach, in feet?

rules_out.why: 64 is the square of the height. The height is the number that multiplies by itself to make 64, which is 8.
4 is 10 take away 6. The three sides of a right triangle do not add and subtract like that, which is the whole reason Pythagoras is needed.
16 would square to 256. The square of the height is 64.

cases.explain: The ladder is the longest side, so its square equals the other two squares added: 100 is 36 plus the height squared, leaving 64, and the height is 8 feet. Notice 10 minus 6 would have given 4, and it is not 4.

given: The ladder is 10 feet long and its foot is 6 feet out, so it reaches 8 feet up.
The window sill is 8 feet up the wall.
The safety rule is that a ladder's foot should stand one quarter of its length out from the wall.
A ladder that is too upright can tip backwards.
debate.question: How many feet from the wall should the foot be? Defend it.

arguments.why: At 6 feet out the top lands exactly on the sill at 8 feet, which is what the job needs.
A quarter of 10 feet is 2.5 feet, which is what the safety rule asks for. It still reaches well above the sill.

debate.note: The geometry is settled and the question is which constraint governs: hitting the sill exactly, or standing the ladder safely. Work out how high it reaches at 2.5 feet before deciding.

cases.title: The Case of the Spreading Rumour
given: On day 1, 4 students had heard the rumour.
On day 2, 8 students had heard it.
On day 3, 16 students had heard it.
The school has 512 students, and the question is day 6.
cases.question: If the pattern holds, how many students have heard it on day 6?

rules_out.why: 24 comes from adding 4 a day. That would put day 3 at 12, and day 3 is 16.
64 is day 5. Day 1 already has 4 students, so the doubling happens five times to reach day 6, not four.
512 is the whole school. The pattern does not reach it until day 8.

cases.explain: Each day the number doubles: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Multiplying by the same factor each step is what makes this exponential rather than linear — a linear pattern adds the same amount each step instead.

given: On day 1, 4 students had heard the rumour.
On day 2, 8 students had heard it.
On day 3, 16 students had heard it.
The school has 512 students, and 180 of them are away on a trip all week.
debate.question: How many will have heard it on day 6? Say what your model assumes.

arguments.why: Doubling from 4 gives 128 on day 6, and nothing in the three days of data breaks the pattern.
With 180 students away, each student who knows has fewer people left to tell, so growth slows before day 6 and something under 128 is the honest figure.
Doubling cannot pass the 332 students actually in the building. The curve has to flatten, and 332 is the ceiling it flattens against.

debate.note: Three days of data fit a doubling and fit the start of an S-curve equally well. Exponential models are always true at the beginning and never true at the end, and naming where yours stops being true is the skill.

cases.title: The Case of the Break-Even Point
given: A shop's weekly profit is 20n - 500 dollars.
n is the number of items sold that week.
The 20 is the profit made on each item.
The 500 is the weekly rent, paid whatever happens.
cases.question: How many items must be sold to break even?

rules_out.why: 500 is a number of dollars of rent. It only becomes a number of items once it is shared out at 20 dollars each.
20 is the profit on one item, which is the rate rather than the count.
480 subtracts 20 dollars from 500 dollars. The 20 is per item, so it cannot simply be taken off once.

cases.explain: Breaking even means profit is zero: 20n - 500 = 0, so 20n = 500 and n = 25. Reading the parts of an expression is the whole skill here — one number is a rate and the other is a fixed cost.

given: Weekly profit is 20n - 500 dollars, where n is items sold.
The 500 rent is charged whether the shop opens or not.
Each item also costs 2 dollars to ship, which is not inside the 20.
Only whole items can be sold.
debate.question: How many items must be sold to break even? Defend it.

arguments.why: The expression the shop uses is 20n - 500, and setting that to zero gives 25. That is the model as written.
Shipping makes the real profit per item 18, not 20, so break-even is 500 over 18, which is 27.8 — and you cannot sell part of an item, so 28.

debate.note: The algebra is identical both times; what changed is what counts as profit per item. Ask whether the 20 was ever checked, because the whole answer rests on it.

cases.title: The Case of the Missing Middle Terms
given: A rectangle's length is x + 5.
Its width is x + 2.
Its area is the length multiplied by the width.
At x = 3 the rectangle measures 8 by 5.
cases.question: What is the area when x = 3?

rules_out.why: 19 comes from x squared plus 10 — multiplying the first terms and the last terms and forgetting the two middle products.
13 adds the length to the width. Area is a product.
26 is the perimeter, twice the length plus twice the width.

cases.explain: Substituting first keeps it honest: 8 times 5 is 40. Expanded, (x+5)(x+2) is x² + 7x + 10, and at x = 3 that is 9 + 21 + 10 — also 40. The 7x is the part that gets dropped.

given: The rectangle's length is x + 5 and its width is x + 2.
A 1-unit border is trimmed off all the way round before use.
At x = 3 the rectangle measures 8 by 5.
Area is length times width.
debate.question: What is the usable area at x = 3? Say what you measured.

arguments.why: The rectangle described in the problem is 8 by 5, and the area of that rectangle is 40 square units.
A 1-unit border takes 2 off each dimension, leaving 6 by 3. The usable area is 18.

debate.note: A trim of 1 unit removes 2 units from each dimension, not 1, and that is where this one is usually lost. Draw it before anybody calculates.

cases.title: The Case of the Hour Already Paid For
given: The plumber charges 50 dollars to come out.
After that he charges 50 dollars an hour.
The bill came to 250 dollars.
There were no parts to pay for.
cases.question: How many hours did he work?

rules_out.why: 5 divides the whole bill by the hourly rate and forgets that 50 of those dollars bought no time at all.
6 adds the call-out charge instead of taking it off. It is already inside the 250.
200 is the dollars spent on labour, not the hours those dollars bought.

cases.explain: Write it before solving it: 50 + 50h = 250. The call-out comes off first because it buys no time, leaving 200 dollars of labour at 50 an hour, which is 4 hours.

given: The plumber charges 50 to come out and 50 an hour after that.
The bill came to 250 dollars.
His price list says the call-out charge includes the first hour of work.
There were no parts.
debate.question: How many hours did he work? Say what your equation assumes.

arguments.why: Taking the charges as two separate things, 50 + 50h = 250 gives h = 4 hours of work.
If the call-out buys the first hour, the 200 dollars pays for 4 more hours on top of it, so he worked 5.

debate.note: Creating the equation is the work, and the price list is part of the problem. Both students solve correctly; only one of them read the small print.

cases.title: The Case of the Lift at Ninety Percent
given: The lift can carry 800 pounds.
The operator riding with the load weighs 200 pounds.
Each box weighs 75 pounds.
The lift must not go over its limit.
cases.question: What is the greatest number of boxes that can go in with the operator?

rules_out.why: 10 leaves the operator out. He is in the lift, and his 200 pounds come off the budget before any boxes go in.
9 boxes is 675 pounds, and with the operator that is 875 — over the limit.
13 adds the operator's weight to the limit instead of taking it away from it.

cases.explain: An inequality, not an equation: 200 + 75b ≤ 800, so 75b ≤ 600 and b ≤ 8. Eight boxes and the operator come to exactly 800, which is allowed; nine would not be.

given: The lift's limit is 800 pounds and the operator weighs 200.
Each box weighs 75 pounds.
8 boxes with the operator comes to exactly 800 pounds.
The safety notice says never load above 90 percent of the limit.
debate.question: How many boxes should go in? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The limit is 800 and 8 boxes with the operator is exactly 800. The inequality is satisfied.
Ninety percent of 800 is 720, and the operator takes 200 of it. That leaves 520 pounds, which is 6 boxes.

debate.note: Hitting a safety limit exactly should make anyone uneasy, which is what the 90 percent rule exists to express. Ask what the limit is for, and whether 800 was ever meant to be reached.

cases.title: The Case of the Chairs That Come in Tens
given: The cost of hiring chairs is C(n) = 25 + 8n dollars.
n is the number of chairs hired.
The 25 is the delivery charge.
The 8 is the price of one chair.
cases.question: What is C(12)?

rules_out.why: 96 is 8 times 12 and leaves out the delivery charge, which is paid once whatever the order.
45 adds the 12 instead of multiplying by it, as though 12 chairs cost 12 dollars between them.
33 is the cost of a single chair plus delivery.

cases.explain: Function notation is an instruction: C(12) means put 12 where the n is. 25 plus 8 times 12 is 25 plus 96, which is 121 dollars.

given: The cost of hiring chairs is C(n) = 25 + 8n dollars.
The 25 is delivery and the 8 is the price of one chair.
The supplier only hires chairs in packs of 10.
The event needs seats for 12 people.
debate.question: What will the hire actually cost? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The function says the cost of 12 chairs, and evaluating it at 12 gives 121 dollars.
You cannot hire 12. The smallest order that seats 12 is 20 chairs, and C(20) is 185.

debate.note: The function has a domain the formula does not mention: it is only defined at multiples of 10. Asking what inputs are actually allowed is the habit worth building here.

cases.title: The Case of the Leak That Slows Down
given: The tank holds 500 litres at the start.
It leaks 12 litres an hour.
Nothing is added to it.
The leak rate never changes.
cases.question: How many litres are left after 15 hours?

rules_out.why: 180 is how much has leaked out, not how much is still in the tank.
488 takes off a single hour's leak. Fifteen hours have passed.
680 adds the leak on. A leak takes water out of the tank.

cases.explain: Build the function before you use it: V(t) = 500 - 12t. At t = 15 that is 500 minus 180, which is 320 litres. The 500 is where it starts and the -12 is what each hour does to it.

given: The tank starts at 500 litres and is measured leaking 12 litres an hour.
Nothing is added to it.
The leak runs slower as the tank empties, because there is less weight of water pushing on it.
The question is about 15 hours from the start.
debate.question: How many litres are left after 15 hours? Say what your model assumes.

arguments.why: A constant rate gives 500 - 12 times 15, which is 320 litres, and 12 an hour is the only rate we were given.
If the leak slows as the level drops, less than 180 litres escapes, so more than 320 is left. The straight-line answer is a lower bound.

debate.note: A linear model is the right first move and it is wrong in a direction you can name. Saying which way your answer is biased is worth more than the answer.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Classes With the Same Mean
given: Class A scored 70, 72, 74, 76 and 78.
Class B scored 40, 60, 74, 90 and 106.
Both classes have 5 students and both have a mean of 74.
The range is the highest score take away the lowest.
cases.question: What is the range of Class B?

rules_out.why: 8 is Class A's range, from 70 up to 78.
74 is the mean, which both classes share. Range exists precisely to say what the mean cannot.
146 adds the highest and lowest scores instead of taking one from the other.

cases.explain: 106 take away 40 is 66. The point of the question is that both classes have a mean of 74 and ranges of 8 and 66: the centre is identical and the spread is not remotely.

given: Class A scored 70, 72, 74, 76, 78; Class B scored 40, 60, 74, 90, 106.
Both have a mean of 74. A's range is 8 and B's is 66.
The pass mark is 65.
The head has to decide which class needs extra help.
debate.question: Which class needs help? Give the spread you are arguing from.

arguments.why: Two of B's students are below the pass mark of 65 and two are far above it. A single lesson cannot serve that spread.
Every student in A sits in an eight-mark band with nobody pulling away. A class learning nothing new together is also a class that needs something.

debate.note: Same mean, different stories, and the mean is what a report usually carries. Have them say what a reader of the mean alone would wrongly conclude.

cases.title: The Case of the Paint That Came Out Exact
given: The wall is 24 feet long and 9 feet high.
One tin covers 130 square feet.
The wall needs two coats.
A door 3 feet by 7 feet is not painted.
cases.question: How many tins does the job need?

rules_out.why: One coat of 195 square feet is a tin and a half. The wall takes two coats.
4 tins comes from painting the whole 216 square feet twice. The door's 21 square feet are not painted at all, let alone twice.
The two coats are already inside the 390 square feet. Doubling the tins as well pays for four coats.

cases.explain: Paintable area is the wall minus the door: 216 minus 21 is 195 square feet. Two coats make 390. At 130 square feet a tin, that is exactly 3 tins.

given: The wall is 24 feet long and 9 feet high.
One tin covers 130 square feet.
The wall needs two coats, and the first coat on bare plaster soaks in.
A door 3 feet by 7 feet is not painted, and the shop sells tins singly with no returns.
debate.question: How many tins should they buy? Defend the number.

arguments.why: 390 square feet at 130 a tin is exactly 3 tins, with nothing bought that is not used.
A first coat that soaks into bare plaster covers less than 130 square feet, so exactly 3 tins will run out somewhere near the end. Buy the spare.
Bare plaster often wants a third coat in patches and the shop takes no returns, so buy for the job you may find rather than the job on paper.

debate.note: The geometry gives exactly 3, which is the most dangerous answer in the room: a model that comes out exact has left itself no room for the thing the model ignored. Ask what each extra tin is buying.

cases.title: The Case of the Triangle on the Globe
given: Two angles of a triangle measure 47 and 68 degrees.
The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
The triangle is drawn on a flat page.
None of its angles is reflex.
cases.question: What is the third angle, in degrees?

rules_out.why: 115 is the two known angles added together. What is left of 180 is the third one.
133 takes only one of the two known angles off the 180.
90 assumes the triangle is right-angled, and nothing in the problem says it is.

cases.explain: The three angles fill a half turn, so the third is 180 take away 47 take away 68, which is 65 degrees. That the three make 180 is a theorem about flat surfaces, which is why the page is mentioned.

given: Two angles of the triangle measure 47 and 68 degrees.
On a flat surface the three angles of a triangle add to 180.
This triangle is drawn on the curved surface of a globe.
On a sphere the angles of a triangle always add to more than 180.
debate.question: What is the third angle? Defend your figure.

arguments.why: On any small patch of the globe the curvature barely shows, and the flat rule gives 65 to within less than a degree.
The surface is a sphere, so the three angles exceed 180 and the third must be above 65. How far above depends on how big the triangle is.

debate.note: The 180-degree rule is not a fact about triangles, it is a fact about flat surfaces, and most students have never been told that it has a condition attached. This is where to say it.

cases.title: The Case of the Tree on the Slope
given: A person 6 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long.
At the same moment a tree casts a shadow 30 feet long.
The sun's rays arrive parallel, so the two triangles are similar.
Both stand on level ground.
cases.question: How tall is the tree, in feet?

rules_out.why: 20 uses the ratio upside down, as if shadows shrank where heights grew.
36 adds the tree's shadow to the person's height, which compares two things that are not alike.
180 multiplies the height by the shadow and never divides, so it is not a ratio at all.

cases.explain: Similar triangles keep the same ratio of height to shadow. The person is 6 to 4, which is 1.5 to 1, and the tree's shadow is 30, so the tree is 45 feet.

given: A 6-foot person casts a 4-foot shadow on level ground.
A tree casts a 30-foot shadow at the same moment.
The tree stands at the top of a slope that falls away from the sun.
A shadow cast down a slope runs further than one cast on the level.
debate.question: How tall is the tree? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The ratio of height to shadow is fixed by the sun's angle, and 30 feet of shadow at 1.5 to 1 gives 45 feet.
The slope stretches the shadow beyond what level ground would give, so a 30-foot shadow belongs to a tree shorter than 45 feet.

debate.note: Similar triangles need the two triangles to sit the same way up on the same flat ground. Naming the condition that fails is more useful than any number here.

cases.title: The Case of the Slice Measured With a Protractor
given: The slice's angle at the centre is 72 degrees.
A full turn is 360 degrees.
The whole circle has an area of 50 square cm.
The slice is a sector of that circle.
cases.question: What is the slice's area, in square cm?

rules_out.why: 50 is the whole circle, and the slice is only part of it.
25 is half the circle. 72 degrees is a fifth of a turn, not a half.
72 is an angle measured in degrees. It cannot also be an area in square centimetres.

cases.explain: A sector takes the same share of the area as its angle takes of the turn. 72 out of 360 is one fifth, and a fifth of 50 square cm is 10.

given: The slice's angle reads 72 degrees on a protractor, out of a full turn of 360.
The protractor can be trusted to about 2 degrees either way.
The whole circle is 50 square cm.
The number is going onto a plan for cutting the slice out of metal.
debate.question: What area should go on the cutting plan?

arguments.why: 72 degrees is the measurement taken, and a fifth of 50 square cm is exactly 10. Inventing extra is guessing.
The angle could be 74, which gives 10.28. Metal cut too small is scrap, so the plan should use the top of the range.

debate.note: Every measured number has a range around it, and which end of the range to use depends on what goes wrong when you are wrong. Ask what happens to a slice cut too big and one cut too small.

cases.title: The Case of the Corner the Surveyor Moved
given: The rectangle's corners are at (1,1), (7,1), (7,5) and (1,5).
Its sides run parallel to the axes.
The length is the difference between the x-coordinates.
The width is the difference between the y-coordinates.
cases.question: What is the area, in square units?

rules_out.why: 20 is the perimeter: 6 and 4 and 6 and 4. It is a distance round, not an area inside.
35 multiplies the coordinates 7 and 5 rather than the side lengths 6 and 4. A coordinate is a position, not a length.
10 adds the two side lengths instead of multiplying them.

cases.explain: Side lengths come from differences, not from the coordinates themselves: 7 minus 1 is 6 across and 5 minus 1 is 4 up. The area is 6 times 4, which is 24 square units.

given: Three corners are recorded at (1,1), (7,1) and (7,5).
The fourth corner is recorded at (1,5), making it a rectangle.
A surveyor went out and measured the fourth corner at (1.4, 5).
The plot is being sold by the square unit.
debate.question: What area should be used for the sale?

arguments.why: The registered plan says the fourth corner is (1,5), and a sale goes on the registered plan: 6 by 4 is 24.
On the ground it is a trapezium with parallel sides 6 and 5.6 and height 4, which is 23.2. The buyer gets the land, not the drawing.

debate.note: Coordinate geometry gives an exact answer to whichever set of points you feed it. Which points are the real ones is a question it cannot answer, and here it is the only question that matters.

cases.title: The Case of the Cone Filled Nearly to the Top
given: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and the same height.
The cylinder holds 54 cubic cm.
Three cones of the same base and height fill the cylinder, so a cone is the cylinder divided by 3.
Both are solid shapes with no gaps.
cases.question: What is the cone's volume, in cubic cm?

rules_out.why: 27 is half the cylinder. A cone is a third of it, not a half, which is worth pouring water to believe.
162 triples the cylinder instead of taking a third of it.
54 is the cylinder itself. The cone sits inside it with room to spare.

cases.explain: Three cones of the same base and height fill one cylinder exactly, so the cone is 54 over 3, which is 18 cubic cm. It is a fact worth demonstrating with rice before it is used as a formula.

given: A cone has the same base and height as a cylinder holding 54 cubic cm, so the cone holds 18.
The cone is being used point-down as a cup.
It can only be filled to a tenth below the rim without spilling.
The liquid in a part-filled cone is itself a smaller cone of the same shape.
debate.question: How much does the cup actually hold, in cubic cm?
